claims: which distinctions between past histories a state keeps and which it erases: why histories that end in the same state are indistinguishable to every later transition, so a distinction no state records cannot be consulted by later rules

how the initial state and the rules together fix which states are reachable, why the same rules started from a different initial state can reach different states, and why a representation can usually express states that no sequence of inputs reaches

the difference between the shared state a protocol's participants must agree on and the private state each participant keeps for itself and others need not agree on, such as its keys, pending messages and view of the others

what decides whether something is an input the machine can receive at all, and why that check can be made without consulting the current state as long as the input set itself is fixed rather than activated by the state, while whether the input is accepted in a given state is decided by the transition rules

why a transition can depend on who submitted an input only through what the input itself carries, such as a sender field or a signature, and not through the channel it arrived by, which a later replay of the inputs does not see
when the order of inputs changes the resulting state: which inputs commute, and why inputs that do not commute make their order part of what has to be recorded with them

why a rule set meant to be deterministic has to define an outcome for every combination of state and well-formed input, including the combinations it refuses, and how a gap leaves implementations free to differ

how a rule set handles a state and input that the conditions of more than one rule match: conditions made mutually exclusive, a fixed precedence among rules, or an ambiguity that implementations may resolve differently

whether the transition rules stand wholly outside the state or are partly held in it, as when deployed code or parameters are stored in state and read by outer rules that stay fixed, and what changes when a transition can alter the rules that govern later ones, including which rules a replay of history has to apply

why whether a machine is deterministic depends on what the model counts as its inputs: a rule that reads a local clock, a random source or an outside system is nondeterministic as modeled, and becomes deterministic when that value is made part of the input or the dependence is removed

why, wherever independent executions of the same rules must agree, determinism has to hold across every implementation, platform and version that executes them, not only within one program, and how a difference among them, such as in arithmetic, iteration order or resource limits, shows up as executions that disagree once an input exercises it

why a deterministic machine cannot by itself produce a value its participants cannot predict, since anyone holding the state and the inputs can compute it, and what that means for rules that need an unpredictable choice

why a model can deliberately leave several next states possible, leaving a choice open to an implementation or the environment, and why replicas that must reach the same state need that choice fixed by the rules or carried in the input

how state machine replication separates ordering inputs from executing them, so that the ordering can sequence inputs it does not interpret, and why every correct replica must then reach the same verdict on ordered inputs that turn out to be invalid

how a client of a replicated machine decides which result to rely on: a reply from one replica can suffice when replicas are assumed only to crash, while under arbitrary faults it needs evidence from more replicas than may be faulty, such as matching replies

why replicas that apply the same sequence of inputs can answer the same query differently at the same moment, since each may have applied a different prefix of it, and how a read is placed in the sequence when it must reflect every write completed before the read began

model.meaning: State is what a system retains of its past at a given moment, the record that its rules consult together with the next input to decide which transitions are valid and what they produce.

parents.state-machines: The parent says what state must capture (whatever can affect a later transition). State adds the converse and its consequences: what a state erases, why histories ending in the same state are interchangeable for every later transition, how the initial state and the rules fix which of the representable states can actually occur, and the line between the state a modeled protocol's participants share and what each keeps privately.
parents.protocols: The parent says state outlasts interactions and carries their consequences forward. State adds which consequences it carries (only the distinctions it records), what bounds the states a protocol can reach, and that the state its rules act on, which every participant must agree on, is not everything a participant holds: keys, pending messages and its view of the others are held privately and may differ without fault.

claims: which distinctions between past histories a state keeps and which it erases: why histories that end in the same state are indistinguishable to every later transition, so a distinction no state records cannot be consulted by later rules

how the initial state and the rules together fix which states are reachable, why the same rules started from a different initial state can reach different states, and why a representation can usually express states that no sequence of inputs reaches

the difference between the shared state a protocol's participants must agree on and the private state each participant keeps for itself and others need not agree on, such as its keys, pending messages and view of the others

placements.state-in-state-machines: Under State Machines the reader has the model (states, inputs, rules) and the criterion for what counts as state. The exposition explains what follows from that criterion (erasure of history, reachability from an initial state, the shared/private line) in terms of a state, a history of inputs and rules, so it extends the parent without restating it and needs nothing specific to this placement.
placements.state-in-protocols: Under Protocols the reader has state as what rules act on and what carries consequences between interactions. The same exposition holds because every claim is stated for any system with rules over a state; the shared/private claim is phrased in terms of a protocol's participants, which is native here, and the reachability and erasure claims need no state-machine vocabulary beyond states, inputs and rules, which the exposition can use on its own terms.

contents: Exactly the distinctions among past histories that some later rule may consult: a balance keeps the amount and erases which transfers produced it; a record of used nonces or processed identifiers keeps whether something was already applied, which is what lets a later rule refuse a repeat.

Two histories that end in the same state are interchangeable for every later input sequence, since rules see only state and input; a distinction the state does not record cannot be recovered by any later rule, and a rule that needs it requires the state to have kept it from the start, unless the distinction can still be derived from a record kept outside the state, as it can when the rules are deterministic and the initial state and past inputs are still available.
Not every kept distinction is useful: a state can keep distinctions no rule consults, so two different states may behave identically; such distinctions are redundant rather than wrong.
fields.producedBy: The initial state, then each valid transition applied to the state before it. Which states can occur is fixed by the initial state together with the rules over the inputs the machine can receive; the same rules from a different initial state (a different starting supply, a different set of initial key holders) can reach a different set of states.
fields.checkedBy: Shared state is checked by participants applying the same inputs to it and comparing the results (how they compare, e.g. through commitments, is not this concept's subject); where the rules are deterministic, any participant holding the initial state and those inputs can recompute it. Participant-held state is checked by no one else: others see it only through the messages and signatures it produces.
fields.lifetime: A state persists unchanged until a transition replaces it; it is the only thing that carries the past into later transitions, so whatever it erased at a transition is gone for every later one.
variants: Shared state: the state the protocol's rules act on and that participants must agree on; disagreement about it means a fault, a fork or a broken assumption.

Participant-held (private) state: what each participant keeps for itself, such as its secret keys (public keys the rules verify against can be part of the shared state), its pending messages and its view of the others; it drives that participant's own decisions, legitimately differs between participants, and is not part of what the protocol requires them to agree on. It is still state in the parent's sense, for the participant's own behavior rather than for the shared machine.
Shared versus private is relative to a group: state two parties keep jointly can be shared between them and private with respect to a wider protocol.

Terminology hazard: elsewhere in MAP 'local state' names the part of the shared state that belongs to one account, contract or participant; the private sense here must not be written as 'local state'. Likewise MAP's Shared State names state several parties can change, as against owned state; the record's 'shared state' means agreed on, so it must say so in one sentence that names Shared State as a different sense without explaining it.
relation: Histories h1 and h2 that end in the same state s are indistinguishable to every later transition: for every input sequence w, the state reached from h1 followed by w equals the state reached from h2 followed by w (under deterministic rules; under nondeterministic rules, the same sets of possible states).

Reachable states = the states obtained from the initial state by any finite sequence of valid transitions on receivable inputs; reachable states are a subset of representable states, and usually a strict one, since an encoding can express values no history produces (a total above a fixed supply, one unique item held by two owners).
A state loaded from outside a history (a snapshot, an imported or migrated state) is not guaranteed to be reachable; conditions argued only over reachable states need not hold for it.
fields.tradeoffs: Keeping a distinction lets later rules consult it but costs storage and enlarges what every participant must agree on; erasing it is cheaper and smaller but removes it from the state, so a later rule that needs it can record it only from then on, unless the distinction can still be derived from a record kept outside the state, as it can when the rules are deterministic and the initial state and past inputs are still available to recompute the state with it included.

design.relationship: State is defined by what it keeps and erases of history (an equivalence among histories), its reachable set is bounded by the initial state and rules (a closure inside a larger representable space), and it has a line, easily blurred, between the shared state participants must agree on and the private state each keeps. The first two are arguments with conditions; the third is a real conflation.

structures.purpose: Separate the shared state a protocol's participants must agree on from the private state each participant keeps (keys, pending messages, its view of the others), so the reader does not treat a node's whole store as protocol state or treat divergence of private state as a fault.
structures.whyNotProse: A participant's store holds both kinds side by side and both are called 'the state', so the conflation is likely and practical: readers judge disagreement in mempools or peer views as forks, or treat private keys as protocol state. Marking the two notions as distinct before the explanation makes the line visible at a glance; a paragraph alone would state the difference without flagging that it is the point most often blurred.

design.division: The prose explains all three claims: why histories ending in the same state are interchangeable and what erasure means for later rules; how the initial state and rules bound the reachable states inside the representable ones and why an unreachable state can still be expressed or loaded; and, after the distinction, what makes state shared (rules act on it, participants validate against it, disagreement is a fault), why private state still drives a participant's own behavior and may differ freely, and that the line is relative to a group. The distinction only names the two notions as distinct (e.g. 'Shared state ≠ Participant-held state'); it must not repeat the explanation, and its labels must not use 'local state', which MAP uses elsewhere for a per-account part of shared state.
design.level: The parent State Machines gives the criterion for what state must capture and the parent Protocols says state carries consequences forward; neither says what state erases, what bounds reachability, or where shared state ends. Those are questions about state itself, not about the model, the rules (Transition Rules), determinism (Determinism) or replication (State Machine Replication), so they belong here. The shared/private line was reserved for state by Protocols and claimed here.
design.territory: Reachability is argued from the initial state and rules without explaining invariants or safety (named only: a condition over reachable states can fail in representable but unreachable ones). How a model chooses what counts as state (state-models), encodes it (state-representation), and what global-state and local-state mean in State & Data are named, never explained, and the private sense avoids the term 'local state'. The initial state is used without explaining genesis. Participants' private views are named, not explained (partial-knowledge, processes). Transitions are used as given by their record (atomic, rule-sanctioned changes), and what makes something an input or how input order matters stays with Inputs; determinism is used only as a condition on the equivalence of histories, not explained.
design.placements: The exposition is written for any system with a state, inputs and rules, and the shared/private claim in terms of a protocol's participants, so it reads as complete at both State Machines and Protocols. It uses no positional reference, does not restate either parent, and the distinction holds at both: under State Machines it separates the modeled shared machine from each participant's own state; under Protocols it separates what the rules act on from what participants hold privately.

audit.note: Re-audit after repair cycle 3 (findings state.md, state-b.md, state-2.md, state-3.md). I read every sentence at both placements, state-in-state-machines (parent State Machines) and state-in-protocols (parent Protocols). The record has a definition, 6 paragraphs and 1 distinction ('Shared state ≠ Private state'), as designed. Earlier findings are all resolved: the owner-list table example now expresses the duplicate; 'secret keys' is used in both places; the unconditioned recompute clause is gone from the distinction; Shared State is named as a different sense without being explained; the converse wording is fixed. state-2 D1 and state-3 D1 are also resolved. Paragraph 2 now reads 'can only begin recording it from then on, unless the distinction can still be derived from a record kept outside the state, as it can when the rules are deterministic and the initial state and past inputs are still available to recompute the state with the distinction included'. The general route (derivation from a record outside the state) is now the exception, and deterministic recomputation is given as one sufficient case ('as it can when'), not a necessary one. That is accurate: deterministic rules plus the initial state and the inputs fix every state the history passed through, so any distinction among histories can be derived. The clause ties back to the paragraph's own 'the inputs may survive in a log or an archive outside the state', and it is consistent with 'no rule reads them there', because the derived distinction re-enters the state rather than being read in place. It is also consistent with the last reachability sentence, since a state recomputed from the initial state under the extended rules is reachable under them. The repair introduced no new defect. It adds no absolute, it does not explain replay or Determinism (determinism stays a condition), and it touches Transition Rules' rule-change claim only through 'a rule introduced later', without saying which rules a replay applies. On parent overlap, the clause applies the State Machines replay fact to a different conclusion (recovering an erased distinction for a later rule) and does not restate it. At Protocols it stands alone. The rest is unchanged and sound. The definition is descriptive, which is acceptable for a lead that must stand at Protocols. Interchangeability is stated for deterministic and nondeterministic rules. Assertions are checkable only against the state. The conservation example gives disjoint reachable sets. A reachable starting point reaches a subset, by transitivity. The width and owner-list examples are representable but unreachable. 'Covered ... only if it is itself reachable' holds. Failure after the same inputs covers the rules themselves. Secret keys and their effects are stated correctly. The two-party balance fits 'relative to a group'. 'Behind rather than in disagreement' is legitimate contextual overlap with State Machine Replication, divided by angle. On representation, the distinction is the designed form; the conflation is real; the prose explains and the block only names the two notions. Canonical at both placements, with no positional words. American English, plain text. Depth follows the three claims, and no point is made twice. Remarks (not defects): (1) Model contents[1] still opens 'cannot be recovered by any later rule ... requires the state to have kept it from the start' before its new 'unless' clause. Read with that clause it is conditioned, and the record is correct. (2) Model variants[0] says disagreement about shared state 'means a fault, a fork or a broken assumption' without 'after the same inputs'. The record states the condition. (3) 'Not every kept distinction is useful ... no rule consults' should be read as the current rules, because the trade-off just before says a kept distinction can serve later rules. Acceptable. (4) The paragraph 2 sentence is long; a matter of taste. (5) Carried from state-3: an assertion attested by a trusted party and checked against a key the state holds is arguably covered by 'kept in some form'. Optional.

resolutions.resolution: 'above' is quantitative ('a total above the token's fixed supply'), not a positional reference. It holds at both placements.
Inputs is used only as a term ('the next input', 'sequence of inputs', 'inputs the machine can receive'). What makes something an input and how order matters are not explained. Named, not explained.

Invariants is named only, in 'arguments about safety and invariants', to say such arguments are confined to reachable states. The token's preserved total illustrates reachability, not what an invariant is or how one is proved. Named, not explained.
Safety is named once alongside invariants as an argument confined to reachable states. What a safety property is or how it is violated is not explained. Named, not explained.

Shared State is named once to mark the homonym: 'which parts of it several parties can change is the separate question of Shared State'. The one-clause gloss matches that concept's title sense. Contention, ordering and ownership are not explained. Named to draw a boundary, as the model's variants[3] requires.

Transitions are used as given ('transitions the rules allow', 'transitions from the initial state'). Their atomicity and what makes one valid are not explained, and nothing overlaps the authored Transitions record. Named, not explained.

Each holds. 'values the rules never produce' is the defining condition of the strict-subset case. 'never creating or destroying any' describes the example token's rules. 'the others need never see it' holds for a secret signing key, since others verify against the public key. 'Starting points are not always that far apart' is a hedge. The cycle-3 clause adds no absolute, and its 'only ... unless' now names the general exception (derivation from a record outside the state), with determinism as a sufficient case.

model.meaning: An input is a discrete item a state machine receives from its environment, such as a transaction or a message, to which the transition rules, applied in the current state, assign the transition it causes, if any.

parents.state-machines: The parent names inputs as one of the model's three parts, places their source, timing and order in the environment, and says that under deterministic rules the input sequence is the more fundamental record. Inputs adds what makes something an input at all (membership in a set the model fixes, decidable without the state) as distinct from being accepted in a given state; that a transition and any replay see only what the recorded input carries, so a submitter's identity can matter only as far as the input carries it; and which part of the order the record must keep: the relative order of inputs that do not commute.

claims: what decides whether something is an input the machine can receive at all, and why that check can be made without consulting the current state as long as the input set itself is fixed rather than activated by the state, while whether the input is accepted in a given state is decided by the transition rules

why a transition can depend on who submitted an input only through what the input itself carries, such as a sender field or a signature, and not through the channel it arrived by, which a later replay of the inputs does not see
when the order of inputs changes the resulting state: which inputs commute, and why inputs that do not commute make their order part of what has to be recorded with them

placements.inputs: The only placement is under State Machines, whose reader has states, inputs, rules, the environment as the source of inputs, and the input sequence as the record from which state is rebuilt. Every claim is stated in those terms (an input set, a state, rules, a recorded sequence and its replay), so the exposition extends the parent without restating it and depends on nothing specific to the placement.

contents: What selects the rules that apply (a kind or type of input) and the arguments those rules use (a payload: an amount, a recipient, a call).

Whatever the rules may consult about the input's origin or authorization: a sender field, a signature over the input, a sequence number. Because the rules consult only the state and the input, under deterministic rules a transition can depend on who submitted an input only through these fields.

Not part of the input unless the model puts it there: the connection, peer or network address it arrived from and the moment it arrived. These are facts about delivery, which the recorded input does not keep.
fields.producedBy: The environment: users, other participants or other systems submit inputs, and the machine has no control over what is submitted or when. The model controls only which submissions count as inputs, by fixing the input set as part of the machine's definition.
checkedBy: Receivability: whether an item belongs to the input set is decided from the item alone (encoding, field types and sizes, a signature that verifies against the key the input itself names). The set is part of the machine's definition, fixed before any state exists, so the check needs no state and anyone can make it, in any state or before any is available; any condition that needs the state is, by construction, a rule.

Acceptance: whether a receivable input is accepted in a given state (enough balance, the expected sequence number, a key the state authorizes for that sender) is decided by the transition rules, which are named here and not explained.

Condition: receivability is stateless while the input set is fixed. Where the accepted formats are themselves activated by the state, as when an upgrade enables a new input type at some height, which set applies depends on the rule version in force; that dependence belongs to Transition Rules and is only named.

The boundary is a modeling choice: moving a state-dependent check into the definition of the input set would make receivability depend on the state, so that participants holding different states would disagree about what is an input at all.
proves: About its origin, an input proves only what it carries in a form the rules can check. A sender field alone is a claim; a signature the rules verify ties the input to the holder of a key (digital signatures are named, not explained).

The channel it arrived by proves nothing to a later replay: replaying, auditing or reproducing state uses the recorded inputs, which do not contain the connection or peer. A rule that consulted the channel would give a different result when replayed, so authorization that rests on an authenticated connection or a trusted peer has to be converted into something the input carries before the input is recorded.
fields.lifetime: Submitted by the environment, checked for receivability, ordered and applied; once applied, the input outlives the moment it was processed as part of the recorded sequence from which state is rebuilt, while everything about its delivery that it did not carry is gone.
relation: Inputs a and b commute in state s when applying a then b from s reaches the same state as applying b then a; they commute unconditionally when this holds in every reachable state. The relation is stated for deterministic rules (named, not explained).

Examples, each assuming the two inputs share nothing the rules check beyond what it names (a sequence number the rules expect from a common sender can make the order matter by itself): transfers between disjoint pairs of accounts commute; two credits to one account commute as long as no limit on the balance can refuse either of them; two withdrawals from one account to different recipients commute in a state whose balance covers both, while in a state whose balance covers each of them alone and not both, whichever comes first is accepted and the other refused; two writes of different values to one key, when both are accepted in either order, do not commute.

Consequence: if every pair of inputs commutes, the set of inputs determines the final state and its order need not be recorded; for each pair that does not commute, their relative order is part of what fixes the result and has to be recorded with them. Because commutation can depend on a state not known when inputs are recorded, a record often keeps a total order.

Commuting in the resulting state is not commuting in everything the machine produces: two orders can reach the same state while reporting different intermediate results, such as which of two operations saw the other's effect.
tradeoffs: Recording a total order of all inputs settles every non-commuting pair without having to identify them, but it also orders inputs that commute without marking which ones do, so applying any of them independently needs that knowledge from elsewhere (parallel execution is named, not explained).

Recording only the order of pairs that do not commute needs every pair that might not commute to be identified when the record is made, for example from inputs that declare what part of the state they touch; where the rules do not confine an input to what it declared, a declaration that omits a part the input touches can leave a non-commuting pair unordered, so replays that order it differently can end in different states.

A narrow, stateless input set lets anyone discard items that are not inputs cheaply and early, but can establish only what the item shows by itself; everything that depends on the state falls to the rules.

design.relationship: Inputs has three claims: a boundary between two checks made at different places (membership in the input set, decided without state, and acceptance in a state, decided by the rules); a causal argument from what a transition and a replay can see to why provenance must be carried by the input; and a condition (commutation) with its consequence for what the record keeps. The first is a real conflation, because 'valid input' names both checks; the other two are arguments with conditions.

structures.purpose: Separate an input the machine can receive (a member of the input set, decided by form without the state) from an input accepted in a given state (decided by the transition rules), so the reader does not treat a malformed item and a well-formed item refused in this state as the same kind of 'invalid'.
structures.whyNotProse: Both are routinely called 'valid' or 'invalid', and the conflation has a practical cost: folding a state-dependent condition into what counts as an input makes receivability depend on the state, so participants holding different states disagree about what is an input. Marking the two as distinct before the argument shows that the boundary is the point; a paragraph alone states the difference without flagging that the shared word is what blurs it.

design.division: The prose explains all three claims: why membership in the input set is decided by form and needs no state (the set is part of the machine's definition), the condition under which that holds (a fixed input set, not one activated by the state) and what goes wrong when a state-dependent check is moved into it; why provenance reaches a transition only through fields the input carries, why the channel is invisible to a replay and why channel-based authorization must be converted before recording; and what commutation is, which inputs commute (with examples, including state-dependent commutation), why non-commuting inputs make their relative order part of the record, and why records often keep a total order anyway. The distinction only names the two notions (for example 'Receivable input ≠ Input accepted in this state'); it must not explain either, and its labels must not use 'valid', the word that conflates them.
design.level: The parent State Machines names inputs as a part of the model and places their order in the environment, but says nothing about what makes something an input, how provenance enters a transition, or which order matters. Those are questions about inputs themselves, not about the rules that accept them (Transition Rules), the fixedness of outcomes (Determinism) or how replicas order and apply them (State Machine Replication), so the representation belongs here.
design.territory: Acceptance in a state is attributed to the transition rules and named, never explained; preconditions, what a refused input produces (invalid transitions) and how messages are validated in a protocol (message validation) are named only. Values such as clock readings or random draws that become inputs belong to Determinism and are not discussed; the provenance claim is limited to who submitted an input. Signatures are named as one field an input can carry, never explained; channels are named as what a replay does not see, not how communication works. Commutation is stated under deterministic rules without explaining determinism, and its use for applying inputs concurrently is named (parallel execution) without explanation. Replay is used as the parent gives it; how replicas order inputs they do not interpret and reach the same verdict on refused ones stays with State Machine Replication. The distinction separates two checks on inputs and draws no sibling's relationship; State's claims (what state keeps and erases, reachability, shared and private state) are not touched.
design.placements: Inputs has one placement, under State Machines. The exposition is written in the parent's terms (input set, state, rules, recorded sequence, replay), uses no positional reference and does not restate the parent; the distinction holds there because it separates two checks on any machine with an input set and rules.

audit.note: Re-audit after repair cycle 1, in fresh context, at the only placement (inputs, leaf under State Machines in Foundations). Findings answered (inputs.md D1-D3, inputs-b.md D1-D7) all resolved: a scoping sentence now states that the examples assume the two inputs share nothing the rules check beyond what each names, with a common sender's expected sequence number as the named exception (A-D1, B-D1); the withdrawals read 'covers each of them alone and not both' (B-D2); the total-order sentence now says it orders commuting inputs without marking which ones do, so applying them independently needs that knowledge from elsewhere, Parallel Execution named only (A-D2, B-D3); the declaration sentence now requires identifying pairs when the record is made and conditions divergence on rules that do not confine an input to the parts it declared and on a declaration that omits a part (A-D3, B-D4); the provenance sentence is conditioned on deterministic rules (B-D5); the channel is 'the one the input first arrived on' (B-D6); 'form' is replaced by 'an item that is not an input' and 'what the item shows by itself' (B-D7); 'conflict' is replaced by 'do not commute' throughout, consistent with the defined term. Model relation, tradeoffs, contents and checkedBy carry the same corrections. Commutation examples re-checked against concrete counter-cases: disjoint transfers with nothing else in common commute in every state (each input's checks and effects read and write only its own accounts; shared fee accounts, global counters or block limits are excluded by the clause and the scoping sentence); credits under a cap L with b+c1+c2<=L commute, with b+c1<=L, b+c2<=L, b+c1+c2>L do not, and a minimum-balance rule (an empty account refusing a small first credit) is also 'a limit on the balance', so 'no limit on the balance can refuse either' is the right sufficient condition; writes of different values both accepted leave the later value, so they never commute, and compare-and-set or max-register semantics are excluded by 'both accepted in either order'; withdrawals x,y to different recipients: b>=x+y both accepted either order (commute), x<=b, y<=b, b<x+y first accepted second refused and the recipients differ even when x=y (do not commute), and the sequence-number counter-case of the first audits is now excluded by the scoping sentence; counter increments by one reach the same count in either order even under a cap (identical effect on the counter) while the values they report differ. The swap argument (s.a.b = s.b.a, deterministic rules carry equality forward), the multiset statement under unconditional commutation (every intermediate state on a swap path is reachable), 'order matters only between inputs that do not commute' (if two orderings end differently, some inverted pair fails to commute in some reachable state), and the receivability, upgrade-condition, provenance and replay paragraphs hold. Parent overlap: none; the record extends the parent's three-part model, its environment-held order and its replay record without restating them. Siblings: State (reachability, erased histories), Transition Rules (rules held in state, named for upgrades), Determinism (named as the assumption only) and State Machine Replication (not explained; replay used in the parent's sense) are not crossed. Structure: the distinction separates two checks that 'valid' conflates; labels avoid 'valid'; prose explains, the block only names. One placement, no positional or time-sensitive words, American English ('the other way around'), plain text. Depth follows the three claims. Remarks: (1) 'participants holding different states ... would disagree about whether an item is an input at all' reads as the risk the design creates; 'could disagree' would be exact, since states that differ only where the moved condition does not look agree. (2) 'Transfers that touch disjoint sets of accounts, and nothing else in common' repeats what the scoping sentence already assumes; harmless. (3) 'Two increments to a counter' relies on increments being unit steps: with different amounts and an upper limit on the counter, the final counts can differ; 'increments by one' would close that reading. (4) Model relation[2] says 'if every pair of inputs commutes, the set of inputs determines the final state'; the record correctly says unconditionally and counting repeats, and the model should match.

resolutions.resolution: Invalid Transitions is named once as where what a refusal produces belongs; nothing about refusal outcomes is explained.
Parallel Execution is named once as the concern of applying commuting inputs independently; how parallel execution detects or uses commutation is not explained.
'rules' is used in the parent's generic sense of a state machine's transition rules; the Protocols concept Rules is not explained.

'state' is used as the parent's vocabulary (current state, reachable state, resulting state); none of State's claims (erased histories, reachability from the initial state, shared vs private state) is explained.
'state machine' appears only in the definition as the parent's term; the parent's model is not restated.
Transition Preconditions is named once with Transition Rules as where acceptance in a state is explained; the record lists acceptance examples only to separate the two checks.
Transition Rules is named for acceptance and for how rules held in the state govern later inputs (upgrades); neither completeness, overlap nor rules-in-state is explained.
'transition' is used as the parent's vocabulary for what an input causes; the Transitions record's content is not explained or restated.

model.meaning: In a state machine, transition rules say, for a state and an input, whether the input is accepted and, if it is, which next state it produces or, where the model leaves a choice open, which next states it allows.

parents.state-machines: The parent names rules as one of the model's three parts and says that, when they are deterministic, the state is a function of the initial state and the inputs. Transition rules add what a rule set must contain for that function to be fixed: an outcome, refusal included, for every combination of state and well-formed input, and a single outcome where more than one rule's conditions match. They also add that part of the rules can itself be held in the state and changed by transitions, so the rules in force are a product of history, and replaying the inputs reproduces the state only if each input is applied under the rules that governed it.

claims: why a rule set meant to be deterministic has to define an outcome for every combination of state and well-formed input, including the combinations it refuses, and how a gap leaves implementations free to differ

how a rule set handles a state and input that the conditions of more than one rule match: conditions made mutually exclusive, a fixed precedence among rules, or an ambiguity that implementations may resolve differently

whether the transition rules stand wholly outside the state or are partly held in it, as when deployed code or parameters are stored in state and read by outer rules that stay fixed, and what changes when a transition can alter the rules that govern later ones, including which rules a replay of history has to apply

placements.transition-rules: The one placement is under State Machines in Foundations, where the reader arrives knowing that a model has states, inputs and rules. The exposition treats the rule set in general terms (completeness, overlapping conditions, where the rules live), names protocol examples such as deployed code and stored parameters only as cases, and does not depend on the parent's wording, so it holds wherever the concept is reached.

fields.contents: For each combination of a state and a well-formed input, a rule whose conditions match it and the outcome it fixes: a next state, or a refusal that leaves the state unchanged. A rule set can define many combinations at once through a default (anything not otherwise allowed is refused), which counts as a defined outcome; silence does not. Where conditions of several rules can match the same combination, the set also carries how one of them is chosen: conditions written to exclude each other, or a fixed precedence among the rules.
fields.producedBy: Written by the protocol's designers as a specification and then realized separately in each implementation, which is where a gap or an unresolved overlap turns into implementations that behave differently. Where part of the rules is held in the state (deployed code, stored parameters), that part is written by transitions themselves, under outer rules that stay outside the state and say how the stored part may be set and how it is interpreted.
fields.checkedBy: Applied by each validating participant for itself to every input it processes; independent implementations agree only on the combinations the rules fix to one outcome. A rule set can be checked for gaps and overlaps by case analysis over its conditions, exhaustiveness checks in its implementation language, model checking, or running several implementations on the same inputs and comparing the states they reach.
fields.lifetime: Rules held outside the state change only when the software every participant runs changes, typically at an agreed activation point, so a history can be governed by a sequence of rule versions, and replaying it means applying each version over the span where it was in force. Rules held in the state change through transitions, and the state at each point carries the version in force, so a replay from the initial state reproduces the right rules as it goes; the outer rules that interpret the stored part still change only in the first way.
fields.invariants: A sound rule set meant to be deterministic fixes exactly one outcome for every state and well-formed input: at least one (no gap) and no more than one distinct outcome (overlaps resolved). When part of the rules is stored in the state, this has to hold for every rule version a transition can install, so the outer rules constrain what can be stored, for example by bounding a parameter to values for which the rules that read it still define an outcome.
variants: Overlap resolution: conditions written to be mutually exclusive, so at most one rule matches any combination.
Overlap resolution: a fixed precedence, so the first or most specific matching rule wins.
Overlap left unresolved: an ambiguity that implementations may resolve differently, a defect rather than a design.

Placement of the rules: wholly outside the state, changed only by changing the software; or partly held in the state, as deployed code or parameters are, and changed by transitions under fixed outer rules.
tradeoffs: Mutually exclusive conditions make each rule readable on its own and independent of order, but each new rule may force the conditions of others to be narrowed; a precedence lets a specific rule override a general one without rewriting it, but a rule's effective meaning then depends on the rules ranked above it that can match with it, and reordering can change behavior.

Holding rules in the state lets them change through ordinary transitions without a coordinated software change, at the cost that the rule applied to an input depends on earlier inputs, and the outer rules that govern the stored part still need the coordinated change.

design.relationship: Conditions and consequences of a specification: the conditions under which a rule set fixes one outcome for every state and well-formed input (no gap, overlaps resolved) and what follows when either fails (implementations free to differ), and the causal chain from rules held in the state to rules that depend on history to a replay that must reproduce the rules in force as well as the inputs.
design.whyProse: Each claim is an argument: why totality, refusals included, is what lets independent implementations agree; how two designs and one defect handle overlapping conditions, and what each costs; why storing rules in the state makes them history-dependent and what a replay must then apply. None is an order of stages, a loop or a set of persistent modes: rule versions move forward and a reversal is another change, so state and flow add nothing. The overlap resolutions are two designs and a defect, not alternatives read across shared dimensions, so a comparison would be a table for its own sake. The one conflation, a refused combination taken for an unspecified one, is real but is settled inside the totality argument in a sentence; a distinction block would restate that sentence rather than show something prose obscures.
design.level: The parent introduces rules only as one part of the model and relies on them being deterministic; whether a rule set is complete, how it chooses among matching rules, and where the rules themselves live are questions about the rule set, so they belong here. They do not belong at Determinism, which owns what the model counts as input, agreement across platforms and versions, and deliberate choice among several next states, nor at Transitions, which owns a single transition's atomicity and composition.
design.territory: The record names, without explaining, Determinism, Specification Ambiguity, Invalid Transitions, Transition Preconditions, Transition Effects, Rules, Transition Functions, Valid Transitions, Rule Changes, Protocol Upgrades, Hard Forks, Protocol Parameters and Contract State. It leaves to Inputs what makes something an input and when order matters, to State what a state retains and which states are reachable, to Determinism how unmodeled inputs and implementation differences cause disagreement and when a model leaves choices open on purpose (an unresolved overlap here is accidental, not deliberate), and to State Machine Replication how ordering is separated from execution. It explains how rules change only as a modeling consequence (rules become state, replay must apply the version in force), not how changes are proposed, activated or governed.
design.placements: One placement, under State Machines in Foundations; the prose states its claims in general terms with protocol cases as examples and does not lean on the parent's sentences, so the single exposition holds there and wherever the concept is reached.

audit.note: Re-audit after repair cycle 2, in fresh context, at the only placement (transition-rules, leaf under State Machines in Foundations); every sentence re-read, not only the repaired ones. Cycle-2 findings (transition-rules-2.md) resolved: E1 the definition now reads 'In a state machine, transition rules say, for a state and an input, whether the input is accepted and, if it is, which next state it produces or, where the model leaves a choice open, which next states it allows', which no longer places the rules in the specification and so fits the outer reading, the inner reading of paragraph 6 (stored code and values in force) and the nondeterministic case Determinism owns; model meaning matches. E2 paragraph 7 now runs position in the order -> which stored version applies -> so the rewriting input can fail to commute, the correct direction (non-commutation is stated within the inner-reading sentence but is not denied for the outer reading). E3 the domain's determinism sentence is no longer restated: 'the stored rules are part of the state, so deterministic outer rules stay deterministic' keeps only the record's own reason. Cycle-2 remarks taken: 'a choice the specification did not make' removes the clash with paragraph 2's implementer choice and paragraph 5's 'resolves the overlap in effect'; 'exercised' replaces 'tested'. Cycle-1 findings (transition-rules.md D1-D7, transition-rules-b.md 1-4) still hold resolved: 'Implementations that conform', 'a router's access control list' (first-match), 'reordering a ranked list can change behavior' (model tradeoffs[0] hedged), the two readings with values included and the inner reading as outer rules plus stored code and values, 'values for which the rules that read it still define an outcome' (model invariants matches), and the refused-versus-unspecified point made once ('unlike a refused combination it is not fixed at all'). No new error introduced by the repair. Accuracy: every universal checked ('every combination' is qualified by the reachable-states sentence; 'at most one rule matches' under exclusive conditions; 'never applies' for a rule wholly shadowed under first-match; 'no transition can change' the outer rules, which sit outside the state; 'has to keep the logic of earlier versions' for software that replays from the beginning); causal direction checked in paragraphs 2, 4, 7 and 8; examples fit (frozen-account and balance rules overlap with different outcomes; first-match ACL; refusal-overrides as outcome precedence; fee rate and size limit as stored parameters; resource-limit failure as a defined result of stored-code execution). One term, one sense: outer rules / stored part / version used consistently. Parent overlap: the State Machines parent mentions rules only as one part of the model and determinism/replay in general; the record adds totality, overlap resolution and layered rules, and its replay paragraph adds which rules a replay must apply, not the parent's replay argument. Domain sentences: the definition necessarily covers 'determine which next states are valid'; the determinism sentence is no longer paraphrased. Territory: Determinism, Specification Ambiguity, Contract State, Protocol Parameters, Rule Changes, Protocol Upgrades and Hard Forks named only; the deliberate-openness contrast in paragraph 5 draws the boundary the design records (accidental vs deliberate) without explaining Determinism's claim; commuting used, not explained, consistent with Inputs, which defers rules held in state to this concept; reachability used, not explained (State); a refusal leaving the state unchanged is the outcome model claim 1 needs, not Invalid Transitions' account; the resource-limit failure is a case, not Transitions' atomicity or Determinism's resource-limit divergence; claims 1-3 each explained (P1-2, P3-5, P6-8). Representation: prose, as designed; no structure buried (no persistent modes with returns, no ordered stages, no shared-dimension alternatives). Placement: single placement valid, no positional or time-sensitive words, identity is the state-machine sense, American English, plain text. Remarks (not defects): (1) 'deterministic outer rules stay deterministic' would read less tautologically as 'the machine stays as deterministic as its outer rules'. (2) Paragraph 2's 'running several implementations ... exposes a gap only when ... the implementations fill it differently' is right about what comparison reveals; 'comparing several implementations' results' would forestall reading it as excluding a gap seen through a crash common to all. (3) Paragraphs 6, 7 and 8 each say the outer rules change only with the software participants run; the paragraph 8 instance bridges to activation, so close to repetition but not a defect. (4) 'Replay separates the layers.' is a thesis sentence, lightly announcing. (5) 'changes what later inputs are accepted or produce' reads better as 'which later inputs are accepted or what they produce'; 'Reproducing it' has a loose antecedent (the original history). (6) 'when it was signed' assumes signed inputs; 'submitted' would be general. Model remarks: checkedBy 'independent implementations agree only on the combinations the rules fix to one outcome' overclaims (they can agree on a gap by coincidence), and lifetime 'the software every participant runs' overstates; the record carries neither.
