model.meaning: Determinism is the property of a state machine, as modeled, that the state and the input it receives fix the next state, so that every correct execution of the same rules from the same state on the same inputs reaches the same result.

parents.state-machines: The parent defines determinism in one sentence (given a state and an input, is the next state fixed?), separates unpredictable inputs from nondeterministic transitions, and states that deterministic rules make state a function of the initial state and the input sequence. Determinism adds what decides whether the property holds and where it ends: that it is relative to where the model draws its input boundary, that it must hold across every implementation that executes the rules and how divergence among them surfaces, that it rules out the machine generating its own unpredictable values, and that a model may leave choices open on purpose, which replicas must then have closed.

claims: why whether a machine is deterministic depends on what the model counts as its inputs: a rule that reads a local clock, a random source or an outside system is nondeterministic as modeled, and becomes deterministic when that value is made part of the input or the dependence is removed

why, wherever independent executions of the same rules must agree, determinism has to hold across every implementation, platform and version that executes them, not only within one program, and how a difference among them, such as in arithmetic, iteration order or resource limits, shows up as executions that disagree once an input exercises it

why a deterministic machine cannot by itself produce a value its participants cannot predict, since anyone holding the state and the inputs can compute it, and what that means for rules that need an unpredictable choice

why a model can deliberately leave several next states possible, leaving a choice open to an implementation or the environment, and why replicas that must reach the same state need that choice fixed by the rules or carried in the input

placements.determinism: The only placement, a leaf under State Machines in Foundations. The exposition explains the property on its own terms for any state machine, so it reads as complete with nothing beneath it and does not depend on the parent's synthesis beyond the vocabulary of state, input and rules; it names no sibling position and no domain-specific context.

fields.statement: A machine is deterministic when its transition is a function of state and input: for each state and each input, the rules fix one outcome. The property belongs to the machine as modeled, with a stated input boundary, and it is only useful to independent executors when every implementation of the rules computes that same function.
establishedBy: rules that read nothing but the state and the input: any value from a local clock, random source or outside system is either removed from the rules or recorded as part of the input, so every executor uses the same recorded value

every implementation, platform and version that executes the rules computing the same function, including where arithmetic, the order of iterating over collections, and resource limits could otherwise differ
each choice a model deliberately leaves open being closed, for replicated execution, either by the rules or by a value carried in the input
violatedBy: a rule that consults a value outside the modeled state and input, such as a local clock reading, a random draw or a query to another system, which different executors obtain differently

implementations that differ in rounding, in the order they visit an unordered collection, or in where they run out of a resource such as memory or stack depth, a difference that stays latent until some input exercises it and then appears as executions that disagree on the resulting state
a choice the model leaves open being resolved independently by each executor
confusions: Deterministic is not the same as predictable by everyone: a deterministic result is predictable by anyone holding the state and the inputs, and unpredictable only to someone missing an input, so a value derived from state alone (a hash of it, for instance) is not a source of unpredictability.

A deliberately nondeterministic model, which leaves a choice open as an abstraction, is not an accidental gap in a rule set; the gap and how overlapping rules are resolved belong to transition rules and are only named.

Determinism as a property of the specified rules is not the same as each program being repeatable on its own: one program can return the same answer every run while disagreeing with another implementation of the same rules.
variants: dependence on the environment: the rule reads a value the model does not count as input
divergence among implementations: the rules are deterministic as written, but executions of them compute different functions
deliberate openness: the model itself permits several next states
tradeoffs: Recording an environmental value as input makes the transition deterministic but moves the question to whoever supplies that input: what it reports and, for a value meant to be unpredictable, whether that party can foresee or steer it.

Leaving a choice open keeps a specification abstract and lets implementations or the environment decide, but replicas that must agree can no longer use the model as written: the choice has to be fixed by the rules or carried in the input.
fields.relation: As a relation, transitions are a set of (state, input, next state) triples; the machine is deterministic when that set is single-valued in its first two components, so next = f(state, input). A nondeterministic model permits several next states for some (state, input) pair; determinizing it means adding the selecting value to the input or a fixed selection to the rules.

design.relationship: Four conditional arguments about one property: its dependence on the model's input boundary, its scope across implementations, its limit (no self-generated unpredictability, with the exposure that leaves), and deliberate nondeterminism in models and what replication requires of it. Each claim is reasoning about conditions and consequences, not an order, branch, loop, persistent states or alternatives read across shared dimensions.
design.whyProse: Each claim turns on a condition (as modeled, across implementations, to someone holding the inputs, where replicas must agree) that a block would strip from its sentence. The sources of nondeterminism are three variants with one consequence each, which a sentence carries; a flow of them would add nothing. The only real conflation, unpredictable inputs versus nondeterministic transitions, is already drawn as a distinction by the parent and must not be redrawn; the confusions this concept adds (deterministic versus predictable by all; deliberate openness versus an accidental gap) are each a clause inside a claim's argument, and the second names a sibling's territory, so a distinction block would either restate the parent or draw a sibling's boundary as this concept's content. There is no process, cycle, state model, tension pair or comparison in the meaning.
design.level: The parent only names the property and its main consequence. What makes it hold or fail, its scope across implementations, its limit on unpredictability and deliberate nondeterminism in models are questions about the property itself, so they belong at this concept rather than at State Machines, Transition Rules (which owns the rule set's completeness and conflicts) or State Machine Replication (which owns how replicas order and execute inputs).
design.territory: Draws no sibling's or reserved relationship. Inputs owns what is receivable and when order matters; this concept says only that a value counts toward determinism when the model records it as input. Transition Rules owns gaps, overlapping conditions and rules held in state; this concept names a gap only to separate it from deliberate openness. State Machine Replication owns ordering versus execution and client trust; this concept says only that replicas need open choices fixed. Deterministic and Non-Deterministic Execution own how execution environments enforce or relax determinism; this concept names sources of divergence, not enforcement techniques. Oracle Problem, Commit-Reveal and Verification are named at most, never explained. The parent's distinction and its replay, audit and reproduction consequences are not restated.
design.placements: One placement, a leaf. Prose that explains the property in general terms for any state machine holds there and reads as complete, with no positional or domain-specific reference.

audit.note: Re-audit after repair cycle 1 (findings determinism.md and determinism-b.md, agreeing). Both findings are resolved. (1) Refinement statement: paragraph 4 now says what is shown for every run the model allows holds for an implementation whose runs are all model runs; resolving each open choice in an allowed way yields only allowed steps, which carries over a safety property (glossed as violated, if at all, at a particular step); a property resting on a fairness condition also needs the resolutions to meet it, with the newest-first scheduler starving an older request as the counterexample. Each clause is accurate, and the causal direction is right. (2) 'open' now has one sense: the input-carried case reads 'keeps any one resolution out of the rules', and the accidental case reads 'leaves a combination unsettled by accident', with no second sense of 'open'. The divergence sentences are merged and the 'first matching entry' example and 'their own reading' are gone. Repair-introduced errors: none found. The rewritten closing sentence on the accidental gap ('needs an outcome fixed for that combination as well, but what was shown of the model need not cover what an implementation does there') is hedged and true, since an implementation step at a gap is not a model step. It states Transition Rules' requirement only as a conclusion, in one clause, reusing the paragraph 2 wording that names the gap as Transition Rules' term, so it is a reference, not an explanation. Whole record re-read against every criterion. Parent overlap (one placement, parent State Machines): the definition necessarily matches the parent's one-line test and adds the outside-value clause. The parent's distinction between unpredictable inputs and nondeterministic transitions is not redrawn, and neither are its replay, audit and reproduction consequences. The domain sentence (independent processes from the same state and inputs reach the same result) is not restated: paragraph 4 makes the opposite, new point that open choices break it. Siblings: State, Inputs, Transitions and Transition Rules are not explained. Paragraph 2's latency of divergence is this concept's own claim 2 (implementations of rules that define one outcome), divided by angle from Transition Rules' gap latency. State Machine Replication's ordering and execution split, client trust and reads are untouched. Excludes (Oracle Problem, Deterministic Execution, Commit-Reveal, Transition Rules, Inputs) are each named only. Structure: prose as designed. The three divergence sources and the three openness examples are variants with one consequence each, so no buried flow, state model or comparison. Accuracy re-verified: FMA contraction, extended intermediates and libm rounding; hash-table order by library, version or seed; resource-limit abandon-versus-apply; producer-set block timestamp; derived randomness foreseeable and grindable; LIFO starvation. Placement: one leaf, no positional or time-sensitive words. Identity: the state-machine property. American English. Depth: 1,226 words, under the long threshold, with each paragraph tied to one claim in order. Remarks (not defects): 'after which they hold different states' (paragraph 2) restates 'part' and could be read as permanent, though reconvergence is possible in principle. The safety carry-over leaves machine closure of the fairness condition implicit, which is standard. The gloss on safety property touches the unauthored Safety concept in one clause only. 'An implementation ... resolves each open choice' sits slightly awkwardly beside the network example, whose choice belongs to the environment.

resolutions.resolution: Commit-Reveal is named once as a scheme addressing who can see or influence a recorded unpredictable value. Its mechanism (commit then reveal) is not described.
Deterministic Execution is named once as the subject that covers how execution environments make arithmetic, ordering and limits part of the rules. No technique is explained.
'execution environments' appears only as a generic phrase in the clause naming Deterministic Execution. It is not explained.

'input' is used throughout as the parent's generic vocabulary. Inputs' territory (receivability, the channel versus carried identity, commutation) is not explained, and 'choose among orderings' concerns steering derived randomness, not commutation.
Oracle Problem is named once, as what the question of a recorded value's worth becomes for facts about the outside world. It is not explained.
'Resource limits' is generic usage: one sentence on implementations exhausting memory or stack differently, which is claim 2's own example. The Resource Limits concept is not explained.
'state' is generic vocabulary. State's territory (erased histories, reachability, shared versus private state) is not explained.
'state machine' appears only in the definition, as the parent's vocabulary. The parent's content is not restated.

Transition Rules is named once to separate a gap from rules that define one outcome. The closing sentence on an accidental gap states only, in one hedged clause, that it needs an outcome fixed and that the model's results need not cover it. Why completeness is required and how gaps make implementations differ are not explained.
'transition' is generic vocabulary (applying, abandoning, checking a transition). Transitions' atomicity and intermediate-state content is not touched.

Five absolutes, each checked. 'cannot by itself produce a value its participants cannot predict' (two uses) follows from the definition: anyone holding the state and inputs computes the same value, and 'by itself' excludes values received as input. 'the holders of the state cannot foresee' states a requirement, not a claim. 'Replicas that must reach the same state cannot rely on that freedom' holds, because independent resolutions can diverge, as the next sentence shows. 'always serves the newest request' describes the counterexample policy, not a claim. All hold.

model.meaning: State machine replication runs copies of one deterministic state machine on several replicas and gives every replica the same agreed sequence of inputs, so that replicas that apply the same prefix of the sequence hold the same state and the service keeps working while some replicas fail.

parents.state-machines: The parent establishes only that, with deterministic rules, the state is a function of the initial state and the input sequence, and that state machine replication is built on this. This concept adds how the property is put to work across replicas: ordering is separated from execution, so validity is decided by every replica at execution rather than by the ordering; a client must decide which replica's reply to rely on, depending on what replicas are assumed to do when faulty; and replicas that agree on the sequence can still be at different points in it, so a read has to be placed in the sequence when it must reflect every earlier write.

claims: how state machine replication separates ordering inputs from executing them, so that the ordering can sequence inputs it does not interpret, and why every correct replica must then reach the same verdict on ordered inputs that turn out to be invalid

how a client of a replicated machine decides which result to rely on: a reply from one replica can suffice when replicas are assumed only to crash, while under arbitrary faults it needs evidence from more replicas than may be faulty, such as matching replies

why replicas that apply the same sequence of inputs can answer the same query differently at the same moment, since each may have applied a different prefix of it, and how a read is placed in the sequence when it must reflect every write completed before the read began

placements.state-machine-replication: The only placement, under State Machines, whose last paragraph names state machine replication as built on replayable input sequences. The exposition explains the replication mechanism itself (ordering separated from execution, the client's choice of reply, the position of reads) without depending on that sentence, and holds for replicated services and blockchains alike because it names the ordering and fault assumptions only as conditions.

sequence: Clients submit inputs (requests or transactions) to the replicated service.
An ordering component, which may be a consensus protocol run among the replicas or a separate sequencer, fixes one sequence of inputs without needing to interpret them.

Each replica applies the inputs whose positions are fixed, in sequence order, to its own copy of the state, checking each against the rules in the state it has reached; an input the rules refuse is still a position in the sequence and is refused identically by every correct replica.

Replicas reply to clients with results once the ordering has fixed the input's position (a design whose replicas reply from a tentative order has the client require more); the client accepts a result according to the fault assumption: one reply from a replica that has applied the input under crash faults, where replicas that recover keep everything they had acted on, or matching authenticated replies from more replicas than may be faulty under arbitrary faults.

Reads are answered from a replica's current prefix, or are placed in the sequence (ordered like an input, or answered only once the replica has applied everything fixed when the read arrived, a position that under arbitrary faults it must learn in a way faulty replicas cannot falsify) when they must reflect every earlier write.
actors: Clients, which submit inputs and decide which replies to rely on.
The ordering component, which fixes the sequence and need not interpret inputs.
Replicas, each executing the same rules over its own copy of the state, some of which may be faulty.
fields.inputs: Client inputs in arbitrary arrival order, the agreed sequence that the ordering produces, the shared initial state and the rules.
fields.outputs: Each replica's state after the prefix it has applied, the result of each input (including refusals of invalid ones), and replies to clients and to read queries.
assumptions: The rules are deterministic across every replica's implementation (owned by determinism; named only).
All replicas start from the same initial state.
The ordering delivers the same sequence to every correct replica (owned by consensus and agreement; named only).

No more replicas are faulty than the design tolerates, and the client's acceptance rule matches the fault assumption (crash faults with recovered replicas keeping what they had acted on, or arbitrary faults with authenticated replies; the fault models are named only).
failures: Replicas that reach different verdicts on an ordered input, through a rule gap or an implementation difference, diverge from that position onward even though the sequence is shared.
A client that accepts a single reply under arbitrary faults can be given a result no correct replica produced.
A read answered from a lagging replica's prefix returns a state that omits writes that had already completed, which matters when the read must reflect every earlier write.
If the ordering lets through inputs that the rules will refuse, the sequence still carries them; filtering spam or malformed inputs is a separate, optional check before ordering.
invariants: Any two correct replicas that have applied the same prefix of the sequence hold the same state.
Every correct replica reaches the same verdict, accept or refuse, on each ordered input.
tradeoffs: Separating ordering from execution lets the ordering run without the state or the rules, but validity can then be known only after ordering, so invalid inputs occupy the sequence.

A single reply is cheap and fast but sufficient only under crash faults; matching authenticated replies from more replicas than may be faulty cost more messages and their authentication but tolerate arbitrary faults.
A read answered from a local prefix is fast but may be stale; a read placed in the sequence reflects every earlier write but costs ordering latency or a wait for the replica to catch up.

design.relationship: A mechanism whose three claims each turn on keeping apart notions a reader is likely to merge: an input being placed in the agreed sequence, every replica having applied it, and the rules having accepted it. The claims explain why each gap exists (validity decided at execution, replicas at different prefixes) and what the client and the reader do about it.

structures.purpose: Show as one chain that an input ordered in the sequence is not thereby applied by every replica, and is not thereby accepted by the rules: Ordered in the sequence ≠ Applied by every replica ≠ Accepted by the rules.
structures.whyNotProse: The three notions are commonly merged into one word, 'committed', and the reader carries that merger into every later paragraph: reading the invalid-input claim as a contradiction and the stale-read claim as a fault. Prose separates them one claim at a time, in different paragraphs; the chain fixes all three as distinct before the prose explains each gap, which prose spread across the record would obscure.

design.division: The prose explains why ordering is separated from execution and why validity, which can depend on an input's position, must be decided identically by every replica at execution; how a client chooses whose reply to rely on under crash and arbitrary faults; and why replicas at different prefixes answer differently and how a read is placed in the sequence. The distinction shows only that ordered, applied by every replica and accepted are three different facts; the prose must not restate the chain as a list, and the chain carries no mechanism.
design.level: The parent names state machine replication only as built on replayable input sequences and draws no line between ordering, application and acceptance; those lines exist only once the machine is replicated and ordering is split from execution, so the distinction belongs here, not at State Machines, and no sibling concerns replicas or clients.
design.territory: The chain is about the replicated mechanism's positions and verdicts, not about how the order is agreed (consensus, agreement and sequencing are named only), not about how a single transition takes effect (transitions, named only), and not about consistency models (named only, as what a read must satisfy). It does not restate the parent's distinction between unpredictable inputs and nondeterministic transitions, and leaves why replicas' implementations must agree to determinism.
design.placements: There is one placement, under State Machines. The distinction and the prose hold for any replicated machine, a replicated service or a blockchain, because they state the ordering and fault assumptions as conditions rather than assuming one protocol.

audit.note: Re-audit after repair cycle 2, in fresh context, at the only placement (state-machine-replication, leaf under State Machines in Foundations). Every sentence was read against criteria 1-6, including those the repair did not touch. Cycle-2 findings resolved: D1, the divergence sentence no longer asserts sufficiency ('Such a split can arise when an input reaches a case that the Transition Rules leave open and implementations fill differently, or a case the rules define but implementations compute differently'), consistent with the Transition Rules and Determinism records; D2, the read requirement is now the umbrella ('answered at a point in the sequence that follows every such write'), so the ordered read's 'a place in the sequence' keeps its narrow sense and the read-index and belief-checking methods meet the requirement without contradiction. Remarks taken: the credit example is conditioned ('unless inputs placed between them credit the account enough to cover it'); the ordered-read inference now states 'had its position, and every position before it, fixed before it completed', which with in-order execution makes 'lands after all of them' valid even where an ordering fixes positions out of order; the repeated crash-rule clause is cut; 'Equal prefixes give correct replicas equal states' restores 'correct'. Model sequence[2] (applies inputs whose positions are fixed), failures[2] (writes that had already completed) and failures[3] (inputs the rules will refuse) are corrected. Cycle-1 findings still hold: the fixed-position assumption governs both reply rules with the tentative-reply caveat unquantified; replies are authenticated as coming from the replica they name; the transferable-signature sentence stays cut; the stale read says 'can return'; equal states rest on initial state and one function, one sequence on the ordering under its fault model and, in many designs, the threshold; crash rule covers recovery with durable state. No new error introduced by the repair: the fee outcome is now 'a transition that takes a fee in place of the requested effect', not a refusal; the cost sentence ('more messages, each authenticated, and a wait for the slowest of the replicas it counts') is accurate. Parent overlap: no sentence restates State Machines' replay paragraph or its distinction; the definition adds correct replicas, prefixes and the fault bound to the domain sentence. Territory: Consensus, Determinism, Transition Rules, Byzantine Behavior, Consistency and the fault model are named, not explained; the replicated outcome for invalid inputs (error result, fee) stays on this side of Transition Rules' completeness claim; authentication is named only. Structure: the Ordered / Applied by every correct replica / Accepted chain is a real conflation ('committed') and the prose explains each gap without listing it. Depth follows the three claims; one placement, no positional or dated words, American English, plain text. Remarks (not defects): (1) the credit example's exception names only inputs between the transfers; a credit placed before both also matters under a fixed-amount reading, so 'unless other inputs credit the account enough before it' would be exact if touched; (2) 'spare the sequence some invalid inputs' after 'malformed inputs or spam' is true of the malformed part, though spam need not be invalid; (3) 'The ordering only has to settle which input occupies which position' is relative to interpretation, the ordering also delivers the sequence as the next paragraph says; (4) model meaning says 'replicas that apply the same prefix' without 'correct', and model parents keeps the narrow 'a read has to be placed in the sequence'; the record is right in both places.

resolutions.resolution: Byzantine Behavior is named once ('as Byzantine Behavior allows') to identify the arbitrary-fault assumption; what such replicas do is not explained beyond the client consequence (a result no correct replica produced), which is this record's claim 2.
Consensus is named once as one form the ordering may take ('may be a Consensus protocol run among the replicas'); how agreement is reached is not explained.
Consistency is named as what specifies what a read must satisfy ('which Consistency models specify'); no model is defined or explained. The read requirement is claim 3's own.

Determinism is named as the subject of implementations computing the rules as one function; the divergence sentence names implementation differences as a cause in one clause without Determinism's catalog of arithmetic, iteration order or resource limits.
Matches the generic phrase 'survives the failure of as many replicas as the design tolerates'; Failures as a concept is not discussed or explained.
Matches 'the fault assumption allows to be faulty'; fault assumptions are used as the condition of the client rule, not explained.

Matches 'under its own fault model'; fault models are named as the condition the ordering's guarantee rests on, with fault classes not explained (crash and arbitrary appear only as the two cases claim 2 names).

Generic use of 'inputs' throughout as what the machine applies; the Inputs sibling's claims (input-set check, sender dependence, commuting inputs) are not explained. 'well formed' and 'malformed' are used only to separate pre-ordering checks from the execution verdict.
False positive from 'which the ordering guarantees under its own fault model' (verb use); ordering guarantees as a concept are not explained, and total order is not described.
Generic use of 'state' as each replica's copy; the State sibling's claims (erased histories, reachability, shared versus private state) are not explained.
Matches 'deterministic state machine' in the definition and the concept's own title; the parent's replay property is not restated, and its distinction is not repeated.

Transition Rules is named as the source of a case left open; the record says the rules must fix one outcome for invalid ordered inputs from the replicated angle (error result, fee) without explaining completeness, precedence or rules held in state.
Matches 'a transition that takes a fee in place of the requested effect', a generic use naming one outcome; how a transition takes effect is not explained.

'which the ordering guarantees under its own fault model' is conditioned on that model and, in many designs, the threshold; 'cannot in general know' is hedged; 'cannot see the state the input will meet' holds for any check made before the position is known; 'cannot falsify' states a requirement on how the last fixed position is learned; 'The guarantee concerns equal prefixes, not equal moments' is scoped to the definition's guarantee. 'must fix one outcome' and 'has to reach the same verdict' are requirements of the replicated design, consistent with Transition Rules.

groupAudit.note: Group audit of state-machines (owned: state, inputs, transition-rules, determinism, state-machine-replication; transitions dual-role, fixed), read side by side against the plan and the parent. Boundaries hold: gaps and overlapping rules are explained only in Transition Rules, which Determinism and State Machine Replication name to separate implementation divergence and invalid-input verdicts from them; open choices are explained only in Determinism, which Transition Rules names as a boundary; commuting is explained only in Inputs, and Transition Rules uses the term in the same sense for a rule-rewriting input; how stored rules govern later inputs is left by Inputs to Transition Rules; equal prefixes and stale reads are developed only in State Machine Replication, while State uses one sentence (behind rather than in disagreement) to define what agreement on shared state is owed about, which its claim needs. Two repetitions follow the claims rather than copying: (1) Inputs (channel and sender authorization) and Determinism (clock, random source, outside system) both conclude that a value outside state and input must be recorded in the input, each for the case the plan assigns it, with Inputs grounding its point in determinism rather than re-explaining it; (2) Inputs and State Machine Replication both use two spends that a balance covers singly but not together, Inputs to show state-dependent non-commutation and State Machine Replication to show that an ordering cannot know validity at the position it assigns; the points differ. No contradictions: valid/accepted/refused, gap, replay, deterministic, commute and shared state carry one sense across members and agree with Transitions (refusal leaves the state as it was; a charged failure is a transition). No template convergence: definitions open differently (State is, An input is, In a state machine transition rules say, Determinism is the property, State machine replication runs), forms differ (prose plus distinction in State, a leading distinction in Inputs, prose only in Transition Rules and Determinism, a three-term distinction chain in State Machine Replication), paragraph counts differ, and no shared enumeration pattern. Several members state a cost or trade-off for each design option; that follows claims that ask how designs choose, not a cloned arc. Zero group signals were printed, so there are no resolutions.
